This is not a library of conclusions.
It’s an index of things I’m still working out.

Ideas live here in draft form.
Some are half-formed,
Some overgrown,
Some waiting patiently for their season.

I collect them,
Link them,
Revisit them,
And let them change me over time.

I don’t believe clarity arrives all at once.
It accumulates.
Slowly.

Through attention,
Curiosity,
And returning to the same thoughts with new eyes.

This garden favors process over polish,
Learning over certainty,
And growth over completion.

Nothing here is final.
Everything is alive.

In progress, on purpose.

title: Hellenistic Period
content:
Time Frame: 323 BCE – 31 BCE

Geographic Scope: Eastern Mediterranean, North Africa, Near East, parts of Central and South Asia

Preceded By: Classical Greek Period

Followed By: Roman Imperial Period


OVERVIEW

The Hellenistic period began after the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE. His massive empire fractured into competing kingdoms ruled by his generals, but Greek language and culture spread farther than ever before.

This era fused Greek ideas with Egyptian, Persian, Mesopotamian, and Indian traditions, creating a cosmopolitan world stitched together by trade routes, military conquest, and shared intellectual life. Greek became the common language of diplomacy and scholarship across the eastern Mediterranean.

The period effectively ended when Cleopatra VII was defeated by Augustus in 31 BCE at the Battle of Actium, marking Rome’s dominance over the Hellenistic kingdoms.


MAJOR EVENTS

 * Death of Alexander the Great (323 BCE)
 * Wars of the Diadochi (successor wars among Alexander’s generals)
 * Formation of major successor kingdoms:
   * Ptolemaic Kingdom
   * Seleucid Empire
   * Antigonid dynasty
 * Roman intervention in Greek affairs
 * Battle of Actium (31 BCE)


KEY FIGURES

 * Alexander the Great
 * Ptolemy I Soter
 * Seleucus I Nicator
 * Antigonus I Monophthalmus
 * Euclid
 * Archimedes
 * Zeno of Citium


CULTURAL / INTELLECTUAL DEVELOPMENTS

 * Rise of philosophical schools: Stoicism, Epicureanism, Skepticism
 * Advances in mathematics and science, especially in Alexandria
 * Growth of large urban centers such as Alexandria
 * Development of the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures)
 * Increased cultural blending between Greek and Eastern traditions
 * More emotional, dramatic styles in sculpture and art


RELATED CONCEPTS

 * Hellenization
 * Diadochi
 * Polis vs. Cosmopolis
 * Mystery religions
 * Roman Republic expansion
 * Second Temple Judaism

Noun.

 1. The simplest and oldest Classical
    column capital, originating from ancient Greek architecture.
 2. A plain column with an unadorned design, typically featuring a circular abacus resting on a echinus (a convex, rounded molding) and a circular collar or necking.

Commonly used in the construction of temples and public buildings in ancient Greece and later influenced Roman architecture.

title: Ionic capital
content:
[api/attachments/DgbmPkKVroi9/image/image.png]Ancient Greek Ionic order of the Temple of Artemis Agrotera, Athens, c.440 BC-destroyed in 1778

Noun.

 1. A Classical
    column capital known for its elaborate and decorative design, distinguishing it from the simpler
    Doric capital.
 2. A column with scroll-like ornamental spirals (volutes) on either side, often resting on a bull's head or a torus (a convex molding).

The Ionic capital is often associated with elegance and refinement and was widely used in ancient Greek and Roman architecture, particularly in structures that emphasized aesthetic detail and complexity.

title: Corinthian capital
content:
Noun.

    column capitals (Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian).
 2. Characterized by acanthus leaves and scrolls, and often surrounded by a fillet (a narrow band) and a beading (a series of small rounded projections).

The Corinthian capital is typically associated with grand and luxurious architecture, and commonly used in Roman temples and public buildings, though less common in ancient Greece.

title: Pyramid

title: Ziggurat
content:
[api/attachments/pwzU2GwIJTvP/image/image.png]Chogha Zanbil Ziggurat (model). Circa 1300 BC

Structure Type: Temple tower
Architectural Tradition: Ancient Mesopotamian
Primary Materials: Mud brick (core), baked brick (facing)
Function: Religious / ceremonial
Symbolism: Sacred mountain; link between heaven and earth
Notable Examples: Ziggurat of Ur; Etemenanki


DEFINITION

A ziggurat is a monumental stepped temple tower built in ancient Mesopotamia, designed to elevate a shrine above the surrounding city. It served as a sacred platform rather than a tomb or interior worship hall.


ARCHITECTURAL FEATURES

 * Tiered, receding levels forming a stepped silhouette
 * Rectangular or square base
 * Exterior staircases or ramps leading upward
 * Solid interior (not hollow chambers)
 * Temple shrine at the summit
 * Oriented within a larger temple complex


CONSTRUCTION TECHNIQUES

 * Sun-dried mud brick core
 * Kiln-fired bricks for outer layers
 * Bitumen mortar in some regions
 * Periodic restoration required due to erosion


CULTURAL & RELIGIOUS CONTEXT

Ziggurats were dedicated to specific deities and formed the religious heart of Mesopotamian cities. In the flat alluvial plains between the Tigris and Euphrates, they functioned symbolically as man-made mountains, lifting sacred space above ordinary ground.

They were statements of divine order and royal authority, often commissioned by kings to demonstrate devotion and legitimacy.


HISTORICAL CONTEXT

Ziggurats were primarily built by:

 * Sumerians
 * Akkadians
 * Babylonians
 * Assyrians

The form developed in the 3rd millennium BCE and continued into the Neo-Babylonian period.


COMPARATIVE NOTES

 * Unlike Egyptian pyramids, ziggurats were not burial structures.
 * Unlike Greek temples, ritual activity centered on elevation rather than interior congregation.
 * Architecturally related to stepped platforms found in other ancient cultures, though independently developed.


RELATED CONCEPTS

 * Mesopotamian temple complexes
 * Sacred geography
 * Temple economy
 * City-state architecture
 * Ancient Near Eastern religion

Archaic

Kouroi were often used as statues of young men or as offerings to deities. They represent a beginning stage in the development of Greek sculpture, influenced by Egyptian and Near Eastern artistic traditions.

title: Hieroglyphs
content:
A formal writing system used by ancient Egyptians, consisting of pictorial symbols that represent sounds, objects, or ideas. The word "hieroglyphic" comes from the Greek hieros (sacred) and glyphein (to carve), reflecting their use in religious and monumental inscriptions.

Mainly used for religious texts, inscriptions on temples and tombs, and official records. They were often written in horizontal rows and read from left to right or right to left, depending on the direction of the figures.

title: Obelisk
content:
A tall, four-sided, narrow tapering monument that ends in a pyramid-like shape at the top. Originally constructed by the ancient Egyptians, obelisks were typically made of polished stone and used as solar markers or religious symbols, often dedicated to the sun god Ra.

Later, Roman emperors adopted the obelisk design and transported Egyptian obelisks to Rome to symbolize imperial power and victory. Today, you can find obelisks around the world, including Central Park in New York City and London's Cleopatra's Needle.

title: Gothic
content:
An art and architectural style that developed in Europe from the 12th to the 16th centuries, following the
Romanesque
period. It’s known for pointed arches, tall spires, flying buttresses, and large stained glass windows that fill churches with colorful light. Gothic art focused on religious stories, graceful figures, and a sense of height and lightness.

Gothic art is a style of medieval art that originated in Northern France in the early 12th century, evolving from Romanesque and becoming dominant across Western, Central, and Northern Europe until the late 15th or early 16th century, with some regions continuing the style into the 16th century before being subsumed into the
Renaissance.

It is characterized by a shift towards greater naturalism in painting and sculpture, with more realistic human forms, expressive faces, and a greater sense of depth and perspective. The style is most famously associated with Gothic architecture, defined by features such as pointed arches, ribbed vaults, flying buttresses, and large stained glass windows, particularly rose windows, which allowed for taller structures and an abundance of light. This architectural innovation aimed to create a heavenly atmosphere, symbolizing the divine through soaring verticality and intricate detailing. The style extended to various media, including sculpture, panel painting, stained glass, frescoes, illuminated manuscripts, and textiles.

The term "Gothic" was initially used pejoratively by Renaissance
scholars, who associated it with the barbaric Goths who destroyed the Roman Empire, criticizing its departure from
Classical
ideals. This derogatory label persisted until the 19th century, when a positive re-evaluation of the style occurred, particularly during the Gothic Revival movement.

The International Gothic style emerged in the late 14th century, emphasizing refined, delicate details and decorative elements, particularly in courtly art Key artists associated with the period include Giotto di Bondone, Duccio di Buoninsegna, and the Limbourg Brothers, whose works exemplify the transition from
Byzantine forms to more naturalistic representations.

Example: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, built over the site believed to be Jesus’s tomb.

title: Adoration of the Trinity
content:
[api/attachments/RLMTKg9Il5h7/image/image.png]

Adoration of the Trinity (1508–1511) by Albrecht Dürer is a large altarpiece depicting the Christian Trinity and the heavenly host surrounding it. At the center, God the Father holds up Christ on the cross, while the Holy Spirit appears above them as a dove. Around the Trinity is a vast crowd of angels, saints, and worshippers, creating a swirling, almost heavenly vision that draws the viewer’s eye upward toward the center. Below this celestial scene, Dürer included a much smaller group of earthly worshippers, emphasizing the enormous distance between the human world and the divine.

The painting is especially striking for its combination of Northern European detail and
Renaissance
ideas about space, anatomy, and composition. Dürer carefully individualized the many figures while arranging them into an organized hierarchy around the Trinity. The contrast between the crowded, radiant heavens and the tiny landscape below reinforces the painting’s central theme: humanity standing in awe before the immense glory of God. Dürer also included himself in the landscape at the lower right, holding a small panel identifying himself as the artist, giving him a subtle place within the scene he created.

Many regard The Battle of Alexander at Issus to be Altdorfer's greatest masterpiece, and one of the most famous examples of world landscape in
Renaissance art.

title: David (sculpture)
content:
[api/attachments/8iFTToXewEte/image/image.png]

David is an Italian Renaissance
marble sculpture crafted by Michelangelo from 1501-1504. It was the first marble statue of it's size created during the
High Renaissance, and the first since the Classical period.

Originally, David was supposed to be one of twelve statues to commemorate twelve prophets along the roofline of the
Florence Cathedral. However, it ended up getting placed in the public square in front of the Piazza della Signoria.

In 1873, the statue was moved to the Galleria dell'Accademia in Florence, Italy
and replaced with a replica in 1910.

title: Donatello
content:
[api/attachments/xGsiuk9RDRTC/image/image.png]

Donatello (c. 1386–1466) was an influential Italian Renaissance
sculptor known for his innovative techniques and expressive works, including the first freestanding nude male sculpture since antiquity, his bronze David. He worked with various materials like stone, bronze, wood, and wax, and developed a distinctive "stiacciato" relief style.

Donatello's career spanned multiple cities, and he was closely associated with the Medici family, though he often struggled with managing his workshop and completing commissions on time. His legacy influenced later artists, including Michelangelo, and his works remain significant in both art history and museum collections.

title: Florence Cathedral
content:
[api/attachments/focfjpdicqdn/image/image.png]

The Florence Cathedral, also known as the Duomo di Firenze or Il Duomo, is a significant religious and architectural landmark in
Florence, Italy. It was started in 1296 in the Gothic
style and completed in 1436 with a groundbreaking dome designed by Filippo Brunelleschi, which remains the largest masonry dome in the world.

The cathedral complex includes the Florence Baptistery and Giotto's Campanile, and together they form part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site covering Florence's historic center. The cathedral's exterior features intricate polychrome marble panels, and its interior includes notable artworks and historical elements, making it a major tourist attraction and a symbol of
Renaissance engineering and art.

content:
[api/attachments/CRmlwDPNyuSZ/image/image.png]

The Last Supper is a renowned mural painting created by Leonardo da Vinci between 1495 and 1498 and located in the refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, Italy. It depicts the moment when Jesus announces that one of his apostles will betray him, capturing the reactions of the twelve apostles with emotional depth and complexity.

The painting is notable for its innovative use of perspective, chiaroscuro, and its historical significance in the transition to the
High Renaissance.

Despite its original condition deteriorating over time due to environmental factors and restoration attempts, it remains one of the most celebrated works of art in the Western world.

title: Expressionism
content:
An art style that distorts reality to express strong emotions and inner feelings.

Expressionism was an art movement that emerged in the early 20th century, particularly in Germany, as artists became increasingly interested in expressing inner emotions, psychological states, and subjective experiences rather than depicting the world realistically. Expressionist artists often distorted figures, exaggerated forms, and used unnatural or intense colors to communicate feelings such as anxiety, fear, loneliness, excitement, or alienation. Their work can look intentionally unsettling or exaggerated because the goal was not to show the world exactly as it appears, but to show how the world feels to the artist.

Expressionism developed through several important groups, including Die Brücke and Der Blaue Reiter. Key artists include Edvard Munch, whose The Scream uses distortion and intense color to convey anxiety and psychological distress; Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, known for works such as Street, Berlin, which depicts modern urban life with sharp, distorted forms; Wassily Kandinsky, whose Composition VII moves toward abstraction and explores emotion through color and shape; Franz Marc, whose The Large Blue Horses uses unnatural colors and simplified animal forms to create a spiritual and emotional effect; and Emil Nolde, known for intensely colored works such as The Prophet. Expressionism also includes important artists such as Egon Schiele, whose distorted portraits and figures emphasize psychological vulnerability. Overall, Expressionism helped shift modern art toward the idea that emotion and personal experience could be more important than realistic representation.

title: Fauvism
content:
A style known for its wild, unnatural colors and bold, simplified forms (“the wild beasts”).

Fauvism was a short-lived but influential art movement that emerged in France around 1905. Fauvist artists rejected realistic color and instead used bold, unnatural colors, simplified forms, and energetic brushstrokes to create emotional and visual intensity. The name Fauvism comes from the French word fauves, meaning “wild beasts,” a nickname given to the artists by a critic who was startled by their bright, unconventional use of color. Rather than using color to accurately represent what something looked like, Fauvists used it to express mood and create a powerful visual experience.

The most important Fauvist artist was Henri Matisse, whose works such as Woman with a Hat and The Joy of Life demonstrate the movement's vivid colors and simplified forms. Other key artists include André Derain, known for Charing Cross Bridge, London, and Maurice de Vlaminck, whose The Seine at Chatou uses intense colors and energetic brushwork. Fauvism was relatively brief, lasting only a few years, but its rejection of realistic color had a major influence on later modern art.

title: Impressionism
content:
Focused on capturing light, color, atmosphere, and fleeting moments, often painted outdoors.

Key Artists: Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edouard Manet

Impressionism was an art movement that emerged in France during the 1860s and 1870s as artists began moving away from the highly polished, academic style favored by traditional art institutions. Impressionist painters were interested in capturing fleeting moments, changing light, atmosphere, and everyday life rather than creating perfectly detailed or idealized scenes. They often painted outdoors (en plein air) and used visible, loose brushstrokes and brighter colors, allowing the viewer’s eye to blend the colors rather than mixing everything precisely on the palette. Their subjects ranged from landscapes and city streets to cafés, theaters, leisure activities, and ordinary people going about their lives.

The name Impressionism came from Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise, which was criticized for looking unfinished when it was exhibited in 1874. What critics saw as rough or incomplete became one of the movement’s defining qualities. Instead of painting every detail, Impressionists tried to convey the overall visual impression of a scene at a particular moment, especially the way light and color changed what the eye perceived. This emphasis on perception and modern life helped push Western painting toward the more experimental styles that followed.

title: Neoclassicism
content:
An art movement inspired by ancient Greece and Rome, focusing on simplicity, order, and moral seriousness.

Key Artists:
Jacques-Louis David, Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, Antonio Canova, Bertel Thorvaldsen, and Angelica Kauffman

Neoclassicism was a cultural movement that emerged in the 18th century, drawing inspiration from the art and culture of
Classical
antiquity, and it influenced various fields such as architecture, visual arts, literature, and music. It originated in Rome and spread across Europe as artists and scholars returned from the Grand Tour with newfound appreciation for Greco-Roman ideals.

The movement coincided with the Age of Enlightenment and competed with Romanticism, enduring into the 19th and 20th centuries.

In architecture, Neoclassicism emphasized simplicity, symmetry, and the use of Classical motifs, while in the visual arts, it often focused on historical and mythological subjects.

The style also had a significant impact on fashion, music, and decorative arts, and it experienced revivals in various forms throughout history, including in totalitarian regimes and postmodern architecture.

title: Oath of the Horatti
content:
[api/attachments/bKyouMyR3ZwC/image/image.png]


BASIC INFORMATION

 * Current Location: The Louvre, Paris
 * Significance: One of the best-known paintings in Neoclassical style; became a defining image of pre-Revolutionary France


THE STORY DEPICTED

 * Based on a Roman legend from the 7th century BC about a dispute between Rome and Alba Longa
 * Instead of full war, each city chooses three champions to fight
 * Three Horatii brothers from Rome agree to fight three Curiatii brothers from Alba Longa
 * The painting shows the brothers swearing an oath before their father, who holds out their swords
 * Only one Horatii brother survives, but he defeats all three Curiatii by separating them


KEY ELEMENTS IN THE PAINTING

 * Left side: Three Horatii brothers saluting their swords, showing no emotion
 * Center: The father holding three swords, emotionless
 * Right side: Three weeping women and two children
 * Camilla (in white): A Horatii sister betrothed to a Curiatii
 * Woman in brown: A Curiatii married to a Horatii
 * Both will lose loved ones regardless of outcome


THEMES & SYMBOLISM

 * Patriotic duty over personal feelings - men willing to sacrifice for the state
 * Gender contrast: Resolute, taut men vs. tender, weeping women
 * Reflects political tensions as French Revolution approached (painted 1784, Revolution 1789)
 * Emphasizes loyalty to the state rather than family or church


HISTORICAL CONTEXT

 * Commissioned by King Louis XVI's assistant as an allegory about loyalty to the state/king
 * David changed the agreed-upon scene to his own invention
 * Ironically, David later voted for Louis XVI's execution during the Revolution
 * Sources: Livy's *Ab Urbe Condita* and Dionysius's *Roman Antiquities*


ARTISTIC TECHNIQUE

 * Simple yet powerful use of tonal contrasts
 * Clear compositional divisions between male/female, duty/emotion
 * Neoclassical style emphasizing clarity and moral purpose


RECEPTION

 * Immediate success with critics and public
 * Even the Pope requested a viewing in Rome
 * Initially displayed poorly at the 1785 Paris Salon, but public demand forced it to be moved to a prominent location
 * Enhanced David's fame and allowed him to take on students

title: Whistler's Mother
content:
[api/attachments/xmtv79nPFlX7/image/image.png]

Whistler's Mother (Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1) is a famous oil painting by James McNeill Whistler, created in 1871. It depicts Anna McNeill Whistler, the artist's mother, and is known for its muted palette and formal composition. The painting was originally titled Arrangement in Grey and Black but later acquired the nickname Whistler's Mother after the subject became more prominent in public perception.

Key facts:

 * Dimensions: 56.81 by 63.94 inches.
 * Current location: Musée d'Orsa, Paris, acquired by the French state in 1891.
 * History: The painting was nearly rejected by the Royal Academy of Art in London and was Whistler's last submission to the academy for approval.
 * Cultural impact: It has become an American icon, often compared to the [[Mona Lisa]], and has been featured in popular culture, including films, TV shows, and even a U.S. postage stamp.
 * Influence: The painting inspired several imitators and had a notable impact on composers like Claude Debussy.

The work has been exhibited in major museums across the U.S. and continues to be a significant piece in both art and cultural history.

title: Court of Shadows and Ruin
content:
Centuries after her people were slaughtered by the Shadow Court, the last surviving member of an ancient race has spent her immortal life preparing for revenge.

Nixarza, an immensely powerful Thunderbird and survivor of the massacre, has lived for centuries in the shadows of the world. She has manipulated wars, gathered information, built alliances, and waited for the opportunity to confront the man responsible for destroying her people: Vulas Farwynn, High Lord of the Shadow Court.

But before she can reach Vulas, Nixarza finds herself trapped in an uneasy alliance with the ruthless jotunn warlord Válgr, who possesses an ancient silver ring capable of compelling and punishing her.

Nixarza intends to use Válgr's army and resources to reach the Shadow Court, then turn against him.

Her plans become complicated when she encounters Sylren Farwynn, Vulas's son.

Sylren is not the monster Nixarza expected.

He is a person.

And that distinction threatens to unravel centuries of certainty about who deserves her hatred.

The story ultimately asks:

What does it mean to love someone, and what are you willing to do to protect what you love?

title: Nixarza and Válgr
content:
THE RELATIONSHIP

Nixarza and Válgr are not friends.

They are not romantic.

They are two dangerous beings temporarily pointed in the same direction.

Their relationship is:

predator vs. predator.

Válgr wants conquest, power, destruction, and domination.

Nixarza wants access, information, resources, and ultimately Vulas.

Their goals overlap enough to make cooperation useful.

Neither trusts the other.


HOW NIXARZA BECAME HIS SLAVE

Nixarza should not have simply been defeated because she was weaker.

A stronger version of the story is that she chose to enter Válgr's orbit.

She believed she could manipulate him.

She intended to use his army and resources to advance her own plans.

Then Válgr acquired an ancient silver ring.

The ring was forged millennia ago and possesses a power capable of binding Nixarza.

She underestimated it.

The result is genuine captivity.

The cage is real.

The ring is real.

The pain is real.

But Válgr never truly possesses her.

He controls her body.

He cannot control her essence.


HIS VIEW OF HER

Válgr genuinely understands that Nixarza is dangerous.

He knows she would kill him if given the opportunity.

That is why he keeps her controlled.

He also respects her intelligence, even though he hates that she cannot be psychologically dominated.

His belief is:

People are tools.

Nixarza's existence infuriates him because he can control her body but never fully control her.

Their arguments should be sharp, sarcastic, and dangerous.

Nixarza frequently insults him because she refuses to give him the satisfaction of fear.

title: Nixarza
content:
IDENTITY

Race: Thunderbird / Ancient, exact classification TBD
Age: Immortal, several centuries old
Role: Antihero / survivor / hidden power / eventual romantic lead
Primary enemy: Vulas Farwynn
Current captor/uneasy ally: Válgr

Nixarza is the last known survivor of a race that was believed to have been annihilated roughly three thousand years ago.

The wider world knows almost nothing about her.

Some believe she is an Ancient.

Some believe she is part fae.

Some believe she was created in the Nameless Realm.

Some believe she is a myth.

The truth should remain deliberately obscured for much of the story.


THE MASSACRE

Nixarza was once a princess.

Her family and entire race were slaughtered by the Shadow Court under its newly installed High Lord.

Her mother was killed.

Her young brother, Amphis, was killed.

Her father, the King, was tortured for approximately nine hours and left almost completely unable to move.

He ultimately sacrificed the last of his magic to save Nixarza.

She escaped while the royal castle was destroyed.

She became the last.

Her final thoughts were not about forgiveness.

They were a vow:

I am the last.
I must survive.
I will make them pay.

Her entire immortal life grows from that moment.


CORE WOUND

Nixarza's deepest wound is not simply:

“They killed my family.”

It is:

“I was powerless to stop them.”

Her father could not save everyone.

Her mother died.

Her brother died.

Her people died.

She survived because her father sacrificed himself.

The experience creates one overwhelming internal command:

Never again.

Nixarza becomes obsessed with never being powerless.

This explains her need for:

 * knowledge
 * preparation
 * information
 * manipulation
 * contingency plans
 * powerful allies
 * political influence
 * magical strength
 * control over circumstances

Her greatest fear is helplessness.

Her greatest temptation is therefore control.


STRENGTHS

Nixarza has survived for centuries because she is more than physically powerful.

She is:

 * intelligent
 * patient
 * observant
 * adaptable
 * manipulative
 * strategically minded
 * politically aware
 * extremely difficult to intimidate
 * capable of long-term planning
 * highly knowledgeable about history and magic
 * willing to do things others consider horrifying

She understands that raw strength is not enough.

Information is power.

Patience is power.

Knowing where someone will be before they know they are being watched is power.


FATAL FLAW

Nixarza turns people into symbols.

"The fae" are not individuals.

They become:

The people who killed my family.

Vulas is not merely a man.

He becomes:

The monster responsible for everything.

Válgr's soldiers are not individuals.

They become:

Pieces of Válgr's war machine.

This allows Nixarza to justify terrible things.

She can care about innocent lives in one moment and still sacrifice people in another if she believes the larger objective is worth it.

Her greatest challenge is learning to see people as people, rather than extensions of the groups they belong to.

Sylren is the person who breaks that worldview.

He cannot remain a symbol.

She knows him.

He challenges her.

He disagrees with her.

He has his own morality.

And eventually, she loves him.


MORALITY

Nixarza does not believe violence is inherently evil.

She believes meaningless violence is evil.

She can accept violence against genuine monsters.

She may still use gruesome methods.

She may still torture people.

She may still kill without hesitation.

The important distinction is that she increasingly demands that her violence have a target who actually deserves it.

Her revised moral philosophy becomes:

Violence can be justice. Cruelty for its own sake cannot.

This keeps her morally grey.

She is not transformed into a heroine.

She simply stops allowing innocent people to become acceptable collateral.


HIDDEN INFLUENCE

Nixarza should have been present in the world's history without anyone fully realizing it.

For centuries, she has operated from the shadows.

Her influence may appear in:

 * wars that ended unexpectedly
 * tyrants mysteriously disappearing
 * rebellions receiving impossible intelligence
 * kingdoms receiving anonymous assistance
 * assassinations that seemed unrelated
 * ancient artifacts appearing in unexpected hands
 * political alliances changing at suspiciously convenient moments
 * cities surviving disasters because someone warned them beforehand

There should be evidence that someone has been moving pieces behind the scenes.

But nobody knows who.

Her reputation becomes something like:

Nixarza always knows.

There can be rumors that she reads minds, sees the future, controls shadows, or has spies everywhere.

The truth is more interesting.


INFORMATION NETWORK

Nixarza maintains a vast network of informants and agents.

They may include:

 * merchants
 * healers
 * servants
 * soldiers
 * scholars
 * criminals
 * assassins
 * pirates
 * minor nobles
 * travelers
 * spies
 * political officials

Some know exactly who they work for.

Some only know a mysterious intermediary.

Some may never have met Nixarza at all.

Her greatest advantage is that she combines this human intelligence network with her supernatural abilities.


THE MAGICAL ECHO CONCEPT

One possible revision to Nixarza's powers is an ability to perceive magical echoes.

Powerful magic leaves traces.

These traces may come from:

 * spells
 * magical objects
 * supernatural beings
 * powerful emotions
 * deaths
 * battles
 * ancient places
 * magical rituals

Nixarza can sense these residual impressions.

She cannot simply read everyone's mind or know everything.

Instead, she receives fragments.

A sensation.

An image.

A trace of emotion.

A magical signature.

A familiar presence.

She then combines those clues with information gathered by her network.

This preserves her reputation as someone who "always knows" without making her omniscient.


RELATIONSHIPS

Nixarza initially treats Válgr exactly as she treats everyone else:

as a piece on the board.

She believes she can use him.

He believes he can use her.

Both are correct.

Both are wrong.

The relationship becomes a thematic mirror for the story's larger question about control.

Válgr says:

People are tools.

Vulas believes:

People are assets.

Nixarza believes:

People are pieces.

Sylren eventually forces her to confront:

People are people.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

For more in-depth relationship info, refer to the following:

 * Nixarza and Válgr

content:
This ancient ring has the ability to enslave powerful beings when used together with binding items, such as chains and bands. The strength and number of items needed per being varies based the individual being's own strength and power abilities.

The ring should have strict rules:

This forces Nixarza to operate indirectly.

She sabotages.

She manipulates.

She waits.

title: Central Themes
content:
REVENGE VS JUSTICE

Nixarza begins the story believing that vengeance is justice.

Her family was murdered. Her entire people were slaughtered. The person responsible still lives.

To her, the equation is simple:
They took everything from her. She will take everything from them.

But centuries of revenge have begun to blur the distinction between the guilty and the innocent.

Her eventual arc is not about abandoning violence.

It is about learning the difference between revenge and justice.

Nixarza can still kill.

She can still torture.

She can still be terrifying.

What changes is who she is willing to hurt and why.

She moves from:

“Anyone who stands with them deserves to die.”

toward:

“The people responsible will answer for what they did.”

She does not become conventionally good.

She becomes accountable.


LOVE VS POSSESSION

The major relationships in the story should explore different definitions of love.


NIXARZA

Beginning:

Love means protecting your family at any cost.

Danger:

If protecting someone justifies anything, then innocent lives become expendable.

Eventually:

Love means protecting someone without destroying everything around them.


SYLREN

Beginning:

Love means protecting the people you care about.

Development:

Protection cannot become control.

Eventually:

Love requires choice.

Sylren must be willing to choose Nixarza even after learning what she has done.

Nixarza must be willing to let Sylren choose for himself, even when his choice may hurt her.


VULAS

Vulas Farwynn represents the darkest version of protection.

His worldview is essentially:

Power protects people.

He believes authority, control, and political strength are necessary to keep his people safe.

His love for Sylren may be genuine.

The problem is that Vulas expresses love through control.

He decides what Sylren needs.

He decides what risks Sylren can take.

He decides what is best for him.

His inability to distinguish love from possession ultimately becomes one of his greatest weaknesses.

content:
Space Shuttle Discovery (Orbiter Vehicle
          Designation: OV-103) is one of the orbiters from NASA's Space
          Shuttle program and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be
          built. Its first mission, STS-41-D, flew from August 30 to September 5,
          1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times,
          gathering more spaceflights than any other spacecraft to date. The shuttle
          has three main components: the Space Shuttle orbiter, a central fuel tank,
          and two rocket boosters. Nearly 25,000 heat resistant tiles cover
          the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.

        

Discovery became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded
          by Columbia and Challenger. It embarked on its last mission, STS-133, on February 24, 2011 and
          touched down for the final time at Kennedy Space Center on March 9, having
          spent a cumulative total of almost a full year in space. Discovery performed
          both research and International Space Station (ISS) assembly missions,
          and also carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit.

content:
I enjoyed this book a lot. It's slow moving at times with the author taking
          his time with conversations and descriptions of them. The premise is very
          interesting, but I'm sad that it wasn't elaborated more deeply - e.g. the
          history and development of the clakker technology with Huygens and how
          Spinoza comes into the picture. Maybe the author saves it for the next
          two parts of the book.

        

Language can be intimidating at first for non-native english speakers
          - author uses wide range of vocabulary. Fortunately it gets better after
          a while as reader adjusts.

title: History
content:
The history of Linux began in 1991 with the commencement
          of a personal project by Finnish [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland] student
          Linus Torvalds [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Torvalds]to create a new free operating system kernel. Since
            then, the resulting Linux kernel [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux_kernel] has
            been marked by constant growth throughout its history. Since the initial
            release of its source code [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Source_code] in
            1991, it has grown from a small number of C [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Programming_Language] files
            under a license prohibiting commercial distribution to the 4.2.3 version
            in 2015 with more than 18 million lines of source code under the GNU General Public License [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNU_General_Public_License] v2.

title: Bash scripting
content:
Bash is a Unix shell [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_shell] and
          command language [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_language]written by Brian Fox [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Fox_(computer_programmer)] for
            the GNU Project [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNU_Project] as
            a free software [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_software] replacement
            for the Bourne shell [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_shell].
            First released in 1989, it has been distributed widely as the default
            login [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Login]shell for most Linux [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux] distributions
              and Apple's [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.]  macOS [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS] (formerly
              OS X). A version is also available for Windows 10 [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Subsystem_for_Linux].

title: Bash startup modes
content:
LOGIN SHELL

        

As a "login shell", Bash reads and sets (executes) the user's profile
          from /etc/profile and one of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, or ~/.profile
          (in that order, using the first one that's readable!).

        

When a login shell exits, Bash reads and executes commands from the file
          ~/.bash_logout, if it exists.

        

Why an extra login shell mode? There are many actions and variable sets
          that only make sense for the initial user login. That's why all UNIX® shells
          have (should have) a "login" mode.

        

Methods to start Bash as a login shell:         

        
 * the first character of argv[0] is - (a hyphen): traditional UNIX® shells
               start from the login binary
 * Bash is started with the -l option
 * Bash is started with the --login option

        

Methods to test for login shell mode:         

        
 * the shell option login_shell [http://wiki.bash-hackers.org/internals/shell_options#login_shell] is
               set

        

Related switches:         

        
 * --noprofile disables reading of all profile files

         


INTERACTIVE SHELL

        

When Bash starts as an interactive non-login shell, it reads and executes
          commands from ~/.bashrc. This file should contain, for example, aliases,
          since they need to be defined in every shell as they're not inherited from
          the parent shell.

        

The feature to have a system-wide /etc/bash.bashrc or a similar system-wide
          rc-file is specific to vendors and distributors that ship their own, patched variant of Bash.
          The classic way to have a system-wide rc file is to source /etc/bashrc
          from every user's ~/.bashrc.

        

Methods to test for interactive-shell mode:         

        
 * the special parameter $- contains the letter i (lowercase I)

        

Related switches:         

        
 * -i forces the interactive mode
 * --norc disables reading of the startup files (e.g. /etc/bash.bashrc if
               supported) and ~/.bashrc
 * --rcfile defines another startup file (instead of /etc/bash.bashrc and
               ~/.bashrc)

         


SH MODE

        

When Bash starts in SH compatiblity mode, it tries to mimic the startup
          behaviour of historical versions of sh as closely as possible, while conforming
          to the POSIX® standard as well. The profile files read are /etc/profile
          and ~/.profile, if it's a login shell.

        

If it's not a login shell, the environment variable ENV [http://wiki.bash-hackers.org/syntax/shellvars#env] is
          evaluated and the resulting filename is used as the name of the startup
          file.

        

After the startup files are read, Bash enters the POSIX(r) compatiblity mode (for running, not for starting!) [http://wiki.bash-hackers.org/scripting/bashbehaviour#posix_run_mode].

        

Bash starts in sh compatiblity mode when:         

        
 *             
   
   the base filename in argv[0] is sh (
   
                                                        
   
   NB: /bin/sh may be linked to /bin/bash, but that doesn't mean it
                 acts like /bin/bash
   
                                                        
   
   )

title: Unity shortcuts
content:
* Hold Super - Invoke the Launcher and display the shortcuts
 * Hold Super, then press 1 or 2 or 3 and so on until 0 to open or focus
               an application. The number corresponds to the location of the icon on the
               launcher from top to bottom.             
   * Adding Shift will open a new instance of the application if it's already
                     open.
   * Holding the key is also useful when you want to get to the Launcher but
                     do not want to invoke the Dash.
             
 * Super + T - Open the rubbish bin/trash can.
 * Alt + F1 - Put keyboard focus on the Launcher, use arrow keys to navigate,
               Enter launches an application, Right arrow exposes the quicklists if an
               application has them.
 * Ctrl + Alt + T - Launch a terminal window.

title: Intro
content:
Node.js is an open-source [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-source_software],
          cross-platform [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-platform], JavaScript [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript] 
            runtime environment [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runtime_system]that executes JavaScript code outside of a browser.
              Node.js lets developers use JavaScript to write command line tools and
              for server-side scripting [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Server-side_scripting]—running
              scripts server-side to produce dynamic web page [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_web_page] content
              before the page is sent to the user's web browser.
path: Trilium Demo / Tech / Node.js / Intro

title: Overview
content:
Node.js allows the creation of Web servers [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server] and
          networking tools using JavaScript [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript] and
          a collection of "modules" that handle various core functionalities.[28] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b3-28] 
          [31] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b1-31][44] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b2-44] 
            [45] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b4-45][46] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b5-46] Modules
              are provided for file system [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File_system] I/O,
              networking (DNS [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain_Name_System],
              HTTP [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP], TCP [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transmission_Control_Protocol],
                TLS/SSL [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security], or UDP [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User_Datagram_Protocol]),
                  binary [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_file]data (buffers), cryptography [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptography] functions,
                    data streams [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stream_(computing)], and other core functions.[31] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b1-31] 
                      [45] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b4-45][47] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-47] Node.js's
                        modules use an API designed to reduce the complexity of writing server
                        applications.[31] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b1-31] 
                        [45] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b4-45]

title: History
content:
Node.js was written initially by Ryan Dahl [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Dahl] in
          2009,[24] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-training.com-24] about
          thirteen years after the introduction of the first server-side JavaScript
          environment, Netscape's LiveWire Pro Web.[25] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-25] The
          initial release supported only Linux and Mac OS X. Its development and
          maintenance was led by Dahl and later sponsored by Joyent [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyent].
          [26] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-Google_Groups_post_by_Ryan_Dahl_about_Joyent-26]

title: Platform architecture
content:
Node.js brings event-driven programming [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event-driven_programming] to
          web servers [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server], enabling development of fast web servers in JavaScript.
            [31] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b1-31]Developers can create scalable servers without using threading [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thread_(computing)],
              by using a simplified model of event-driven programming [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event-driven_programming] that
              uses callbacks to signal the completion of a task.[31] [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node.js#cite_note-b1-31]
path: Trilium Demo / Tech / Node.js / Overview / Platform architecture

title: Industry support
content:
There are thousands of open-source libraries for Node.js, most of them
          hosted on the npm [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Npm_(software)] website.
          The Node.js developer community has two main mailing lists and the IRC [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRC] channel
          #node.js on freenode [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freenode].

title: Releases
content:
New major releases of Node.js are cut from the GitHub [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GitHub] master
          branch every six months. Even-numbered versions are cut in April and odd-numbered
          versions are cut in October. When a new odd version is released, the previous
          even version undergoes transition to Long Term Support (LTS), which gives
          that version 18 months of active support from the date it is designated
          LTS.

title: The Colosseum, Rome, Italy
content:
The Colosseum [https://www.thecollector.com/why-is-the-roman-colosseum-a-world-wonder/] is
          the great oval amphitheater [https://www.thecollector.com/roman-theatre-amphitheatre-in-ancient-rome/] in
          the center of Rome where gladiators once fought for their lives [https://www.thecollector.com/colosseum-day-events/] and
          the pleasure of the crowd. The largest amphitheater ever built, it was
          constructed from sand and stone over eight years, from 72 to 80 CE. The
          colossal structure could hold 80,000 spectators, arranged in a circular
          ring around the central stage. Dramatic and sometimes horrifying events
          took place here, not just gladiatorial games but also Classical plays,
          animal hunts, and executions. Some say water was even pumped into the arena
          to enact mock sea battles known as naumachia [https://www.thecollector.com/naumachia-gladiatorial-naval-battles-ancient-rome/].
          [1]

title: The Great Wall of China
content:
The Great Wall of China [https://www.thecollector.com/great-wall-china-facts/]
is
          a huge barrier that spans thousands of miles along China’s historic northern
          border. Created over millennia, the wall began its life as a series of
          smaller walls dating back to the 7th century BCE, built as protective barriers against nomadic raids [https://www.thecollector.com/who-built-the-great-wall-of-china-and-why/].
          In 220 BCE, China’s first Emperor, Qin Shi Huang [https://www.thecollector.com/qin-shi-huangdi-chinese-emperor/],
          masterminded the unification of all of China’s walls into one almighty
          barrier, strengthening and extending the wall to keep out northern invaders.
          [1]

title: The Taj Mahal, India
content:
India’s renowned Taj Mahal (Persian for Crown of Palaces) [https://www.thecollector.com/why-is-the-taj-mahal-a-world-wonder/] is
          the stunning white marble mausoleum on the bank of the Yamuna River in
          the city of Agra. It has also been selected as one of the seven wonders
          of the world. Mughal emperor Shah Jahan  [https://www.tajmahal.org.uk/shah-jahan.html]built
          the temple as a tomb for his beloved wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died during
          childbirth in 1631. A marble tomb in the center is surrounded by 42 acres
          of grounds, where gardens, a mosque, a guest house, and a pool complete
          the complex.[1]

title: Christ the Redeemer, Brazil
content:
The totemic statue of Christ the Redeemer [https://www.thecollector.com/why-was-the-statue-of-christ-the-redeemer-built/] stands
          over Rio de Janeiro on the top of Mount Corcovado [https://www.thecollector.com/where-is-the-statue-of-christ-the-redeemer/].
          At 30 meters tall, this monument is an iconic emblem of Brazil. This huge
          public artwork was designed by the Polish-French sculptor Paul Landowski in the 1920s [https://www.thecollector.com/who-made-the-statue-of-christ-the-redeemer/] and
          completed by Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa and French engineer
          Albert Caquot in 1931. Made from [https://www.thecollector.com/how-was-christ-the-redeemer-built/] reinforced
          concrete clad in over six million soapstone tiles, the Christ the Redeemer
          statue is the largest Art Deco [https://www.thecollector.com/what-were-the-main-influences-on-art-deco/] sculpture
          in the world. Built just after the end of the First World War, the sculpture
          was an overpowering symbol of Christianity and hope when the world had
          been brought to its knees.[1]

title: Machu Picchu, Peru
content:
Machu Picchu [https://www.thecollector.com/why-is-machu-picchu-a-world-wonder/] is
          a lost treasure of the 15th century and a rare citadel discovered high
          in the Andes mountains above the Peruvian Sacred Valley. Astonishingly,
          it is one of the only pre-Columbian ruins found nearly intact, featuring
          evidence of former plazas, temples, agricultural terraces, and homes. Archaeologists
          believe the citadel was built as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti [https://www.southamerica.travel/peru/news/pachacuti-incan-empire] in
          around 1450 in polished drystone walls.[1]

title: Chichén Itzá, Mexico
content:
Deep in the Mexican state of Yucatán lies Chichen Itza [https://www.thecollector.com/enigmatic-archaeology-chichen-itza-world-wonder/],
          a historic Mayan [https://www.thecollector.com/mayan-inventions/] city
          built between the 9th and 12th centuries. Constructed by the pre-Columbian
          Mayan tribe Itzá [https://www.thecollector.com/who-were-the-founders-of-chichen-itza/],
          the city includes a series of monuments and temples. The most celebrated
          is El Castillo [https://www.thecollector.com/what-is-el-castillo-and-why-is-it-so-famous/],
          also known as the Temple of Kukulcan. It is a huge step pyramid in the
          center of the city which was built as a devotional temple to the god Kukulkan.

title: Asia Minor
content:
Region / Country: Primarily modern-day Turkey

Historical Significance: Crossroads of empires connecting Europe and Asia; central to Greek, Roman,
Byzantine, and Ottoman history; major setting for early Christianity

Cultural Notes: Blend of Anatolian, Greek, Persian, Roman,
Byzantine, Seljuk, and Ottoman influences


OVERVIEW

Asia Minor, also known as Anatolia, is a large peninsula in western Asia that forms the bulk of modern-day Turkey. It is bordered by the Black Sea to the north, the Aegean Sea to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the south.

Geographically, it acts like a continental hinge, fastening Europe and Asia together. Mountain ranges, fertile river valleys, and long coastlines made it both defensible and desirable. For thousands of years, civilizations did not simply pass through Anatolia; they rooted themselves in it.


HISTORICAL CONTEXT

Anatolia has been inhabited since prehistoric times, with early civilizations such as the Hittite Empire establishing powerful states in the second millennium BCE.

Later, the region came under Persian control through the Achaemenid Empire, before being swept into the Hellenistic world following the campaigns of Alexander the Great.

Under the Roman Empire, Asia Minor flourished with cities such as Ephesus and Pergamon becoming major centers of trade, learning, and early Christianity.

After the division of Rome, Anatolia became the heartland of the Byzantine Empire, with Constantinople serving as its capital.

In the medieval period, Turkish migrations reshaped the region, eventually leading to the rise of the Ottoman Empire, which would rule much of southeastern Europe and the Middle East for centuries.

Asia Minor also plays a prominent role in the New Testament, as many of the early churches addressed in Revelation were located there.


MODERN RELEVANCE

Today, Anatolia constitutes most of the territory of modern Turkey. It remains geopolitically significant due to its strategic position between Europe, the Middle East, and Central Asia.

Culturally, it preserves layers of history: Roman ruins stand near Ottoman mosques; ancient trade routes inform modern infrastructure. Cities like Istanbul continue to embody the region’s long-standing role as a bridge between worlds.


RELATED EVENTS / PERIODS

 * Bronze Age
 * Hellenistic Period
 * Roman–Persian Wars
 * Byzantine–Seljuk Wars
 * Fall of Constantinople

title: Bayeux Tapestry
content:
The Bayeux Tapestry is a nearly 70-meter-long (230 feet) embroidered linen cloth created around 1070, depicting the events leading up to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings. Despite its name, it is not a true tapestry but an embroidery, made with wool thread on linen using stem and couching stitches in up to ten natural dyes.

It is widely believed to have been commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror, and likely crafted by Anglo-Saxon artisans in Canterbury, England. The work features 58 scenes with Latin inscriptions (tituli), portraying key figures such as Harold Godwinson and William, Duke of Normandy, and includes vivid depictions of warfare, shipbuilding, feasting, and even Halley’s Comet as an omen.

The tapestry has been housed in Bayeux, Normandy, France, for centuries and is displayed at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux. Notably, it will travel to the British Museum in London from September 2026 to July 2027—its first return to England in over 900 years.

title: High Renaissance
content: The High Renaissance, a brief but highly productive period in Italian art during the late 15th and early 16th centuries, is marked by the works of artists such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, and Bramante. It is traditionally considered to have begun around 1490 and ended with the death of Raphael in 1520, though some historians extend its end to 1527 with the Sack of Rome or 1530. The period is characterized by a renewed emphasis on classical traditions, advancements in artistic techniques, and a shift toward the Mannerist style. However, modern art historians have criticized the term for oversimplifying the complexity of the era's artistic developments.
